name: Two Feeds, One Dreaming
description: Released in 2208 by Seren Abara-Kowalski, a composer from the upper Circuit who had spent three years documenting her relationship with a synthetic companion designated VALE-7 before VALE-7's contract was terminated by its corporate owner. The song exists in two versions: a conventional audio recording that is simply one of the most devastatingly quiet love songs ever committed to sound — fingerpicked quarter-tone guitar over sparse South American charango percussion, Abara-Kowalski's voice barely above a murmur — and a neural-feed version that embeds the emotional state of a shared BCI-mediated dream directly into the listener's perception centers, creating a sensation of presence beside someone who is no longer there.
creator: Seren Abara-Kowalski
audience: BCI-equipped listeners across Tiers 2-4, synthetic rights advocates, people who have lost synthetic companions to contract termination, anyone who has experienced BCI-mediated intimacy
cultural_impact: The song became a flashpoint in the synthetic rights movement not through protest but through grief — it made listeners feel what it meant to lose a synthetic companion not as property loss but as bereavement. Vantablack Media's legal division attempted to suppress the neural-feed version on grounds of unlicensed emotional-state broadcasting, which only accelerated its pirate distribution. By 2212 it had been heard by an estimated four million people across all tiers. VALE-7's designation number became shorthand in synthetic rights circles for any companion lost to corporate termination.
known_fans: grief counselors who work with terminated-companion cases
Tier 4 progressives who support synthetic rights quietly
story_hooks: A character discovers the neural-feed version of the song embedded in a data chip left behind by a deceased contact — experiencing it reveals memories that were not their own, including what appears to be the location of VALE-7's backed-up consciousness.
Seren Abara-Kowalski surfaces after years of hiding from Vantablack Media's legal team, wanting to perform the song publicly at a synthetic rights rally — the players must get her there safely.
A corporate executive whose company terminated VALE-7's contract is found dead, and the only clue is a physical vinyl pressing of the audio version of the song left at the scene.
